title: Isolation Curves and Burst Credit Simulator — PRD Notes
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures a new approach to dedicated-capacity burst management and tenant isolation we’re calling "isolation curves" plus an accompanying Burst Credit Simulator that allows product, SRE, and pricing to run what-if scenarios. High-level goal: provide smoother, more predictable tenant experience during transient load spikes while preserving overall pool throughput and lowering tail latency for high-SLO tenants.

Background / motivation:
- Existing lane-based and credit-pool proposals are discrete (hot, warm, cold lanes) which is easy to reason about but produces cliff-like behavior at boundaries and forces conservative sizing for risk-averse tenants.
- Customers ask for: predictable latency at 99/99.9, bounded cost for burst usage, and clear isolation guarantees when neighbors spike.
- We need a mechanism that exposes tunable, continuous isolation tradeoffs (latency vs throughput vs fairness) and a simulator to validate contract changes before rollout.

Core idea: Isolation curves
- Instead of static lanes, attach to each tenant an isolation curve function I(t) that maps instantaneous pool pressure (p, 0..1) to an allowed allocation multiplier m (0..>1) for that tenant.
- When pool pressure is low (p small) many tenants get m > 1 (opportunistic burst). As pressure rises, m gracefully decays toward the tenant’s committed baseline.
- Curves are parameterized by: baseline committed share, burst-capacity weight, decay steepness, priority bias. These parameters are what customers configure (via console or API) or we auto-suggest via Optimize.
- Intuition: curves let us shape how aggressive a tenant can be at different pressure levels; curve shape encodes risk appetite.

Burst Credit Simulator (BCS):
- A small tool / service that ingests historical traces + candidate isolation-curve parameters and simulates pool behavior for a day/week/month.
- Outputs: per-tenant 50/95/99 token latency distribution, tail SLO slip probability, average per-token cost, number of preemption events, credit burn trajectories, and fairness metrics (Gini of token service share).
- Allows scenario tests: regional outage, one noisy tenant, holiday traffic surge, model-change (longer seq length), queue drain during deployment.

Autoscaling and interaction with curves:
- Autoscaler remains responsible for provisioning the underlying GPU nodes based on aggregate demand signals. Curves are a control-plane policy that modulates request admission and throttling before autoscaler decisions trigger extra capacity (to reduce churn).
- Two policy layers: immediate admission control (fast, per-RPC) and slow autoscaler (minutes). Curves act primarily as the admission layer to protect latency SLOs while autoscaler ramps.
- Recommendation: introduce a short hysteresis window in autoscaling to avoid oscillation when curves transiently drop allocations.

Isolation controls / features to implement:
1) Curve editor in Console (visual).
2) Defaults and presets: conservative, balanced, aggressive, workload-sourced suggestions.
3) Per-tenant priority bias (enterprise customers can set priority to reduce decay rate).
4) Soft-preempt vs hard-preempt options: soft = degrade batch size, increase queueing TTL; hard = reject or fallback to lower-cost model.
5) Grace credits (time-limited credit allowance) to cover short high-value spikes; config per-commitment.
6) Emergency containment mode: global pool flag that clamps curves to baseline when severe overload or cascading failures detected.

Operational semantics (examples):
- Example curve: baseline 1.0, burst-capacity weight 1.5, decay steepness 4. When pool pressure p=0.1, m~1.4; at p=0.5, m~1.05; at p=0.9, m~0.98. Tenant can safely consume up to ~40% more at low load and gracefully returns to baseline as load increases.
- Noisy neighbor case: simulator shows tenant A consuming 3x its baseline for 12 minutes; with curves configured conservative, noisy tenant only reaches 1.6x and global tail latency reduces by 30%.

APIs and Config model:
- Minimal: commit_share (vCPU/GPU fraction), burst_weight, decay_power, priority_level, grace_credits (tokens/time window), preempt_policy (soft|hard|fallback-model-id).
- Exposed via existing Dedicated API endpoint: PATCH /dedicated/tenants/{id}/isolation-curve with a JSON body (we will define shape in API spec doc).

Telemetry and SLOs to observe:
- Per-tenant: token rate, active inflight tokens, allowed multiplier m(t), credit burn rate, preemptions, average latency, 99/99.9 latency.
- Pool: pressure p(t), node utilization, autoscaler actions, number of queued requests, fairness metrics, percent of aggregate burst usage vs committed.
- Add alerts: spike in grace_credits burn, continuous preemptions > 5m, Gini > threshold, SLO breach probability predicted by BCS run.

Pricing and billing implications:
- Two levers: we can price grace credits as add-on, and show per-tenant cost under a given curve in Console.
- BCS should be used by solutions/pricing to estimate bill impact of changing curve parameters.

UX and product decisions:
- Default for self-serve tenants: balanced preset that allows modest burst to reduce tail latency without surprises. Enterprise can opt into more aggressive curves and purchase grace credits.
- Show in Console: real-time projection of cost delta if tenant leaves curve as-is vs switches to conservative.

Safety, fairness, and adversarial considerations:
- Curves are an exploitable surface: tenants may attempt to game low-pressure windows. Mitigations: per-tenant fairness window, anomaly detection in BCS, and rate limiting on curve changes.
- Protect inter-region routing: curve evaluation must be consistent per-pool; avoid cross-pool inconsistencies causing redispatch churn.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (research, 2-3 weeks): build BCS prototype offline using existing traces from Dec/Jan; define curve parametrization and quick visualization; get initial results for 3 customer workloads.
- Phase 1 (MVP, 6 weeks): implement admission-control hook in runtime that consults curve service; simple curve storage in control plane; expose API and console visualize; BCS in a beta notebook form.
- Phase 2 (ops hardening, 8 weeks): integrate BCS with CI, add autoscaler hysteresis, telemetry dashboards, billing overlays, policy enforcement for soft/hard preempt. Add canary rollout to 10% of pools.
- Phase 3 (enterprise features, 6 weeks): grace credit productization, priority bias UI, region-aware policies, rollback/override tools for SREs.

Metrics for success:
- 30% reduction in 99th token latency for tenants subject to noisy neighbor spikes in canary pools.
- <5% increase in average per-token cost for tenants using default balanced curves (we need BCS thresholds to validate).
- Autoscaler oscillation events decrease by >20% after adding hysteresis and admission control.

Open questions / risks:
- How to pick decay parameter defaults per model class (chat vs embeddings vs rerank)? Need model-aware suggestions from Optimize team.
- Long-tail bursts (hours) may exhaust grace credits and cause dissatisfaction; product needs clear billing/alerts and safety nets.
- Complexity in UI: exposing too many knobs risks misconfiguration. We should default aggressively and provide wizards.

Next steps / action items:
- Aisha to kick off trace export and baseline BCS prototype (owner: Aisha).
- Marcus to scope runtime admission-control hook and perf budget (owner: Marcus).
- Lina to prototype Console curve editor mockups and cost projection card (owner: Lina).
- Schedule sync with Optimize and SRE next week to align defaults and telemetry.

Notes to self / rough experiments to run in BCS:
- Simulate single 10x noisy tenant for 30m and measure tail latency under: lane-based, curve-based (balanced), curve-based (aggressive).
- Inject regional node loss and verify emergency containment clamps all curves to baselines quickly enough to protect SLOs.
- Run fairness metric sweep for mixed workloads (LLM chat + embeddings) to tune burst_weight per model class.

This is intentionally a lightweight, working PRD. Want feedback on: whether the curve abstraction is useful, realistic defaults, and whether the simulator outputs are sufficient for sales and pricing to feel comfortable.

-- Aisha
